title: Max Bill, Junghans kitchen clock with timer, 1956
lede: A kitchen wall clock designed by Max Bill, with Ernst Moeckl, while he directed the Ulm School: a pale blue ceramic body, a white dial with thin grotesque numerals, and a timer below.
summary: Pale blue drop-shaped body, white dial with thin numerals and fine ticks, and a round timer. Max Bill for Junghans, 1956.

creator.name: Max Bill and Ernst Moeckl, designers; Junghans, maker

made: Designed 1956; the V&A also gives 1960–1970 for this example

evidence.note: Inspected the V&A’s primary image 2007BP8871 of object M.224-2007 at 1067 × 1600 px, through the V&A IIIF service.

styles.note: Made by the school’s first rector during his Ulm years. The dial follows Ulm discipline, but the curved, colored body does not.

context: The V&A says the clock “was designed by Max Bill whilst Director of the Hochschule für Gestaltung (HfG Ulm)”. It gives glazed earthenware, glass, chrome, painted metal, plastic, and a quartz mechanism, a design date of 1956 with Ernst Moeckl, and Junghans, Schramberg, as maker. [V&A M.224-2007](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O164396/).
The record describes the body as “coloured a pale blue” outside and white inside, moulded in an inverted “V” shape. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O164396/).
observed: The body is a glossy pale blue shape like a rounded drop, wide at the top.
The white dial carries thin, light grotesque numerals 1 to 12, fine minute ticks, and small “JUNGHANS” capitals with wide spacing.
The hands are plain black strips with pointed ends, around a small white disc.
A round white timer dial below has small numerals every five minutes and a pale cream pointed knob.
interpretation: The dial is the Ulm part: thin type, an exact scale, and no decoration. The color and the curved body belong more to general 1950s domestic design, so the clock is a bridge object and not a core example.
borrow: Set a scale with thin numerals and fine, even ticks, and let the scale be the decoration.

rights.statement: Image © Victoria and Albert Museum, London, under the V&A’s own terms, not an open license. Max Bill died in 1994, so the design is protected in Switzerland and Germany. No image is stored.
